Interpreter
in-TUR-pruh-ter
noun
From the Latin interpres, a broker or go-between, hence one who explains — inter, between, with a root sense of trading or bearing across. In the AV it renders the Hebrew luts / melits (a spokesman, an intermediary) and the Greek diermeneutēs.

Biblical Definition

An interpreter is one who carries a meaning across — from a tongue not understood, from a dream, from God to men. Scripture’s governing statement on the office is Joseph’s in the prison house. The butler and baker say they have dreamed and there is no interpreter of the dream, and Joseph answers, “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (Gen 40:8). He does not deny that he will interpret; he denies that the interpretation is his. Pharaoh later summons him on report that he can understand a dream to interpret it (Gen 41:15), and Joseph answers the king in the same terms: it is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Daniel says the same before Nebuchadnezzar. Elihu speaks of a rarer office still — “a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness” (Job 33:23) — a mediating voice that declares to a dying man what God is doing with him, which the New Testament fulfils in the one Mediator. And Paul lays the rule upon the assembly: “if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church” (1Co 14:28). The gift of a tongue without interpretation is not permitted to occupy the congregation. Meaning belongs to God; the church is to be edified, not impressed.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who explains or expounds; one who translates from a tongue not understood; a go-between who carries a meaning across.

expand to see more

INTERPRETER, n. [L. interpres, a broker, an agent between parties.] One that explains or expounds; an expositor.

One that translates from one language to another for the understanding of the hearers.

One who declares the mind of God to men — “an interpreter, one among a thousand” (Job 33:23).

In the church, the one without whom a tongue must be kept silent (1Co 14:28).

Joseph and Daniel are the great scriptural instances, and both refer the interpretation to God (Gen 40:8; Dan 2:28).

Key Scripture

Gen 40:8 — "And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you."

Gen 41:15 — "And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, that thou canst understand a dream to interpret it."

Job 33:23 — "If there be a messenger with him, an interpreter, one among a thousand, to shew unto man his uprightness:"

1Co 14:28 — "But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God."

Modern Corruption

Postmodern hermeneutics relocates meaning from the text to the reader — “the text means what it means to me” — making every man his own interpreter and no man accountable to God’s own sense.

expand to see more

The reigning error of the age is reader-response interpretation: the claim that a text has no fixed sense of its own, that meaning is produced by the reader’s community and situation, and that to speak of what a passage means apart from what it means to someone is naive. It arrives in the church as the small-group question — “what does this verse mean to you?” — and as the sermon that begins with the text and ends with the preacher. Peter forecloses it: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:20–21). The reasoning is exact. Because the origin of Scripture is not private, its interpretation cannot be private. Joseph said it before Peter did: interpretations belong to God. The interpreter’s task is to find the sense God put there, not to supply one, and the sense is single — the plain, grammatical, historical meaning the Spirit intended, which the Confession makes the rule for settling every controversy.

The mirror error is the priesthood of the specialist: meaning locked away with the scholar, the guru, or the anointed leader who alone can unlock it. Scripture answers both with the perspicuity of the Word and the illumination of the Spirit. The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily to try even an apostle’s preaching, and were called noble for it. The rule of faith is that Scripture interprets Scripture: the infallible rule of interpretation of Scripture is the Scripture itself, so that when there is a question about the true and full sense of any place, it must be searched by other places that speak more clearly. Keep Paul’s discipline too. Where there is no interpreter, silence — because a church may not be occupied with utterance no one can weigh. Edification, not ecstasy, is the measure of everything said in the assembly, and the man who cannot be understood is to speak to himself and to God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin interpres, a go-between; one who bears a meaning across from God’s mind to man’s.

expand to see more

Interpreter — Latin interpres, a broker or agent between parties.

Hebrew melits (H3887), a spokesman or intermediary — Job 33:23; Gen 42:23.

Hebrew pathar (H6622), to interpret a dream — the Joseph narratives (Gen 40–41).

Aramaic peshar — Daniel’s word before Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar.

Greek diermeneutēs (G1328), the required interpreter of a tongue (1Co 14:28).

Usage

"“Do not interpretations belong to God?” is the charter of the office — and its limit."

"Paul forbids uninterpreted tongues in the assembly; edification governs every utterance."

"Scripture interprets Scripture: the clearer places settle the sense of the darker."
